name: Measuring tape
lead: A flexible measuring tape is a ribbon of cloth, fibreglass or plastic marked with a centimetre or inch scale, used to record circumferences such as the waist, chest, upper arm and thigh. In physique and appearance tracking it complements the bathroom scale: a falling waist measurement alongside stable or rising chest and arm measurements is read by practitioners as a sign of fat loss with muscle retention or gain. Tracking this way lets people see changes that body weight alone cannot show, and so adjust training and diet toward a leaner, more muscular look.[1][6]

Tailors' sewing tapes, now typically fibreglass because it resists stretching and tearing, are the traditional form of the tool, and Wikipedia notes they are used mainly to measure the waist line.[6] The tape itself has not been the subject of gadget-specific trials. Its use rests on the broader field of anthropometry, in which waist circumference is a standard clinical indicator of abdominal adiposity with published risk thresholds for type 2 diabetes and metabolic syndrome.[1][2]
Measurement reliability depends on landmark, tension, posture and operator, and this has been studied in settings ranging from human clinical practice to veterinary muscle assessment.[3]

paras: Tape measures are designed for specific trades and scales. Wikipedia describes sewing tapes as originally cloth or plastic, with fibreglass now preferred; carpentry and construction tapes use a curved metal ribbon that stays stiff when extended and retracts into a case, and surveying tapes may use invar for low thermal expansion.[6] Rigid retractable tapes are distinct from the soft, non-stretching tapes used for the body.

Body tapes are usually cloth, fibreglass or coated plastic, because the material must wrap around curved surfaces and resist stretching under tension. Some versions have a spring-loaded retractable case and a lock to hold the loop at a fixed length, and some have a gauge to help apply consistent tension.

The European Commission has a non-compulsory accuracy classification for tapes, with Classes I, II and III; for a 10 m tape, tolerances are about 1.1 mm, 2.3 mm and 4.6 mm respectively.[6] Body-measurement tapes are short enough that this class difference is small relative to technique error.

Before standardised tapes, tailors used unmarked cloth tapes that were notched by hand to record clients' proportions. Wikipedia credits the British metalworker James Chesterman with the first retractable tape measure in 1821, a spring-loaded cloth strip in a case, and later with a steel tape made from surplus flat wire as pannier dresses fell out of fashion.[6] William H. Bangs received a patent for a spring-return tape measure on 6 December 1864, improved by Alvin J. Fellows in 1868, and Hiram A. Farrand patented the concave-convex steel tape in 1922, the basis of modern pocket tapes.[6] Another account credits Chesterman with patenting a steel tape in 1829.[4] These histories concern general-purpose tapes; the soft body tape descends from the tailor's tool.

Practitioners record circumference at a fixed anatomical site, often the narrowest point of the waist or the navel level, the largest part of the relaxed or flexed upper arm, the chest at nipple level and the thigh at a set distance from the knee. Repeating the same sites on a regular schedule produces a series of numbers that can be set against weight and photographs.

The rationale given in training communities is that body weight alone cannot separate fat from muscle, whereas girth at selected sites can move in different directions. Changes in waist circumference are used as a proxy for abdominal fat, and growth in limb circumference as a proxy for muscle, provided measurements are taken under consistent conditions.

Wikipedia's waist-circumference article notes that waist measurement appears to predict adverse outcomes better than body mass index, and that weight lifters can have a high BMI but low cardiovascular risk, so waist size may be more informative for them.[7]

Wikipedia describes several conventions. The strict World Health Organization landmark is midway between the lowest palpable rib and the top of the hip bone (iliac crest). A practical alternative is the smallest circumference of the natural waist, usually just above the navel, and for a convex abdomen the level one inch above the navel. It notes that measuring at the navel can lead to underestimates, that posture should be kept constant, and that self-reported waist sizes tend to underestimate, with greater error at larger sizes.[7] Waist-to-hip ratio, waist circumference divided by hip circumference, is used to describe fat distribution, and a 2007 meta-analysis reported that both waist circumference and the ratio predicted cardiovascular events.[7]

subs.h: Waist circumference as a health indicator
paras: A 2009 review in the Journal of Diabetes Science and Technology described waist circumference as a reliable biomarker of type 2 diabetes risk, and discussed how cut-offs differ between populations; U.S. goals cited waist below 89 cm for women and 102 cm for men (the NHLBI high-risk lines are above 88 and 102 cm), whereas Japan set lower thresholds for older adults.[1][7] The review suggested that action thresholds might be set more stringently than current U.S. guidelines.[1] A 2004 review of central obesity and the metabolic syndrome likewise treated central adiposity as a core feature used in screening.[2]

A scoping review of muscle-mass assessment in dogs found limb circumference to be the most commonly used modality, in 55 of 62 articles, and noted that factors such as tape type affect reliability.[3] This is veterinary research, cited as an illustration that tape-based girth measurements are sensitive to technique. A single-surgeon series used a standard measuring tape to document breast-surgery outcomes at preoperative and one-year postoperative visits, finding consistent changes in landmark distances after each procedure type.[5]

The tape poses no physical risk, but readings vary with tape height, tension, breathing phase, posture and time of day, and may differ by centimetres between operators. A circumference does not distinguish fat from muscle by itself. Clinicians who work with body-image concerns note that frequent measuring can be associated with preoccupation with the body; for that reason, tracking is commonly done at set intervals rather than continuously.

No studies found on measuring tapes as a self-tracking gadget for appearance. Related research exists on the tool's clinical use: waist-circumference thresholds for diabetes risk and metabolic syndrome are reviewed in the medical literature,[1][2] and limb-circumference reliability has been reviewed in veterinary muscle assessment.[3]

angle.text: A measuring tape gives numbers for waist, chest, arms and thighs that can move in different directions even when scale weight stays flat. People use these numbers alongside photos to see whether a cut or bulk is changing their proportions.
